R01.overview: Dash prepares arithmetic-garbled CNN computation ahead of evaluation. Its LabelTensor representation carries encoded numeric values through layers, separating one-use garbling and label distribution from the evaluator's online arithmetic work.
R01.reading: For PLLM, distinguish the paper's CNN evaluation and setup costs from any adapted decoder operator; related arithmetic-garbling components are bounded references, not the full Dash system.

R02.overview: ReDASH tackles fixed-point scaling in arithmetic-garbled inference, where values move between residue-number-system encodings without losing signed meaning. Its ScaleQuant+ policy treats the scale schedule and the protected conversion between representations as separate costs alongside circuit evaluation.
R02.reading: PLLM has bounded numeric conversion primitives, but not ReDASH's complete scaling protocol. Compare exact rounding, sign handling, and conversion cost before claiming equivalence.

R03.overview: Garbling Gadgets develops arithmetic-label constructions alongside Boolean garbling. Linear arithmetic on labels and nonlinear or cross-modulus gadgets have different ciphertext, freshness and security contracts; a working gadget does not by itself supply a private inference protocol.
R03.reading: PLLM's CRT-garbled multiplication adapts some of these ideas for bounded Q7 regions; functional truth tables alone do not establish security for an entire inference protocol.

R04.overview: Half Gates cuts the ciphertext cost of garbled-circuit AND gates while retaining free XOR. Its two-ciphertext gate construction reduces a Boolean circuit's communication, but input labels, circuit setup and fresh-use requirements remain part of evaluation.
R04.reading: PLLM has bounded half-gate reference primitives, not a reviewed full-model Boolean backend. Count circuit freshness and the complete gate stream when comparing costs.

R05.overview: LogRow privately looks up a value using a masked row index and one-hot garbled labels rather than one full encrypted row per possible input. A random function hides table values from the evaluator; the masked index, fresh labels and masked table bits still contribute to the full communication cost.
R05.reading: PLLM now has a bounded, in-process Rust reference for 1–9-bit tables and the fitted Q7 SiLU table, with a one-element semantic SiLU binding for Qwen2/Qwen3 plans. It uses the earlier two-row One Hot Garbling setup rather than LogRow's optimized one-row setup, so its material size is not the paper's optimum. It has no Python execution API, remote protocol, tensor schedule, full-decoder integration, or security review; compare full material, input/output labels, setup CPU, and numeric fidelity before choosing it as a serving component.

R06.overview: Duty-Free Bits studies conversion from Yao-style Boolean labels to projective or affine representations for other garbling schemes. The conversion direction, algebra and relation to vector OLE matter independently of the garbled arithmetic performed after the bridge.
R06.reading: This is relevant to crossing Boolean and arithmetic regions, but it does not supply a free bidirectional conversion or a drop-in protected decoder runtime for PLLM.

R07.overview: Slalom partitions neural inference between a trusted execution environment and an untrusted accelerator. Masked linear delegation, secret Freivalds checks and the enclave trust boundary are separate ingredients; removing the attested boundary changes the security claim even when the algebra matches.
R07.reading: PLLM's prepared masking and Freivalds verification use a trusted client and a separate preparation role instead of reproducing Slalom's TEE deployment. Their trust and performance claims must be evaluated independently.

R08.overview: Carnival explores masks derived from public knowledge to reduce preprocessing costs for outsourced linear inference. The public-basis mask preparation and private-input leakage resistance are separate obligations; a later attack finds a subspace witness for one vulnerable construction.
R08.reading: PLLM implements the bounded public-mask subspace leakage witness from Maverick Appendix E as an independent assurance control; Carnival remains a research target, not a default preparation choice, and the witness does not cover every mask variant.

R09.overview: HyCC compiles a program into regions using different secure-computation protocols rather than forcing every operation through one backend. Its region assignment must account for conversion between private representations; without that cost, a locally faster operator may make the complete program slower.
R09.reading: For PLLM, typed operator and privacy contracts must constrain any placement search; a candidate should include conversions, setup, memory, and traffic before comparison.

R10.overview: These protocols evaluate a decision program without revealing the selected path in the same way as an ordinary branch traversal. Oblivious transfer supports protected choices over a fixed decision structure.
R10.reading: Applying the technique to decoder lookups would require separate accounting for public depth, visible topology, path access, and arithmetic input/output conversion.

R11.overview: Factored edge-valued binary decision diagrams compress repeated subfunctions using additive and multiplicative edge factors. The contribution concerns representing a function with fewer graph nodes, not hiding its inputs by itself.
R11.reading: PLLM could compare equivalent public lookup graphs by node count and compile memory, then measure protected execution separately; graph compression is not a privacy guarantee.

R12.overview: Piranha organizes secure computation into reusable GPU kernels, distributed protocols and applications. Its kernel acceleration is distinct from multi-party scheduling: transfer, inter-party communication and all participants' work still determine end-to-end cost.
R12.reading: A kernel port into PLLM would not make a two-party online protocol into a one-evaluator private-inference composition. Compare full protocol and device costs.

R13.overview: SIGMA combines preissued function-sharing keys with protected transformer operators and GPU-oriented execution. Dealer key issuance, each online share holder's nonlinear work and whole-decoder state are distinct requirements; a single-party table lookup cannot reproduce the system.
R13.reading: For PLLM, a fair comparison fixes model, token workload, all roles, and key traffic; a single forward pass does not establish sustained autoregressive decode.

R14.overview: FuseFSS studies fusion of helper and nonlinear work in function-secret-sharing-based LLM inference. Its fused schedule must be compared with an equivalent unfused FSS operator using the same fresh keys, online parties and numeric policy; surrounding protected computation does not vanish.
R14.reading: A PLLM adaptation would compare the complete fused sequence, fresh keys, widths, and online dependencies under the same multi-party topology.

R15.overview: Ring PCG constructs pseudorandom correlation generators over integer rings, including multiplication-related correlations. The seed/key setup and expansion into correctly shared ring OLE material precede any private arithmetic that consumes it; compact seeds alone do not establish a cheaper protocol.
R15.reading: Such a generator is not a generic compressor for garbled tables. PLLM would need correct ring identities and attack-aware parameters before treating it as a preparation option.

R16.overview: Trapdoored matrices provide structured pseudorandom material for delegated linear algebra under an LPN-based approach. Private trapdoor setup and the outsourced matrix operation are distinct pieces; the trapdoor and code parameters determine both efficiency and what a server may infer.
R16.reading: PLLM cannot replace the construction with a convenient public low-rank mask: nullspace projections would leak information. Any adaptation needs separate correctness and leakage evaluation.

R17.overview: Curl represents private nonlinear functions with wavelet-encoded lookup tables and discusses probabilistic truncation. Compressed function encoding, private selection and fixed-point rescaling have separate cost and accuracy contracts; none becomes free merely because the table representation shrinks.
R17.reading: For PLLM, measure protected access, conversions, setup, and numeric accuracy on the same model; a stand-alone truncation argument is not a whole-session security claim.

R18.overview: Compact builds piecewise polynomial approximations for costly private activations using public knowledge of the input distribution. Offline interval calibration, hidden interval selection and protected polynomial evaluation are distinct operations; scalar fit error does not establish decoder generation quality.
R18.reading: A PLLM candidate would need protected interval selection, truncation, range checks, and full-checkpoint quality evidence before serving as an alternative nonlinear component.

R19.overview: The available abstract describes outsourcing open-weight LLM inference to two malicious, non-colluding servers with public information supplied by the model owner. It claims both privacy and verifiability, but the abstract alone does not supply enough protocol detail to reproduce those claims.
R19.reading: This remains source-acquisition-gated in PLLM; do not interpret abstract performance language as a measured autoregressive benchmark.

R20.overview: Oblivious ciphertext compression uses linear codes and syndrome decoding to reduce protected payloads under a stated input domain. Correct recovery depends on that domain and side information; an arbitrary ciphertext stream is not necessarily compressible without loss.
R20.reading: PLLM would need explicit out-of-domain collision cases, encoder/decoder costs, and matched uncompressed controls before using the technique on protocol messages.

R21.overview: NEXUS combines approximate homomorphic encryption for linear work with lighter garbled-circuit operations in non-interactive two-party transformer forward inference. The HE–garbling conversion is a separate protected boundary; forward evaluation does not by itself cover persistent decoder state or token-by-token feedback.
R21.reading: A PLLM LLM-serving adaptation would have to implement and measure KV state, recurrent token generation, and the complete conversion boundary separately.

R22.overview: BumbleBee provides a two-party framework for large transformer inference, including specialized protected nonlinear work. Both parties remain online holding shares across the operator graph; a forward-transformer result does not by itself establish cached autoregressive decoding.
R22.reading: For PLLM, this is a different trust topology from one-evaluator serving. Repeated generation without a cache is not evidence of sustained cached decode.

R23.overview: MPCache studies static and dynamic KV-cache eviction to reduce protected attention work. Compiler-side eviction rules, private selection of retained state and the three-party execution of subsequent attention are separate requirements; its SecretFlow/SPU artifact measures operators rather than a complete private serving stack.
R23.reading: PLLM adapts cache eviction as a model-neutral plan transformation, but transformed state and protected attention do not yet execute together end to end.
